specPoints.text: be able to construct Born-Haber cycles and carry out related calculations

primer.text: Lattice energy cannot be measured in a single experiment, so a Born-Haber cycle assembles it from steps that can. This note draws the cycle for sodium chloride level by level, applies Hess's law in the form delta-latt = delta-f minus the sum of the element-to-gaseous-ion steps, and calculates lattice energies for potassium chloride and magnesium oxide from given data.

lessons.title: Building the cycle level by level
sourceHeadings: Drawing the cycle for sodium chloride
lessons.opening: A Born-Haber cycle is Hess's law dressed for ionic compounds: energy climbs the diagram, elements sit a third of the way up, and each enthalpy step carries the chemistry to gaseous ions and back down to the lattice. Sodium chloride walks every level: atomise both elements, ionise one, feed electrons to the other, then close with formation and lattice energy.
keyPoints: A Born-Haber cycle applies Hess's law to ionic compounds and enables lattice enthalpy to be calculated where no direct experiment exists.
Energy increases going up the diagram; the elements in their standard states sit about a third of the way up on a marked starting level.
Creating gaseous atoms is bond breaking, so those arrows point up: sodium +108 kJ mol^-1, half Cl2 +121 kJ mol^-1.
Ionisation continues upward: Na losing an electron costs +500 kJ mol^-1; electron affinity descends: Cl gaining an electron releases -364 kJ mol^-1.
The enthalpy of formation, -411 kJ mol^-1 for NaCl, sits at the bottom with its arrow pointing down for an exothermic change.
Lattice enthalpy, usually shown as formation, closes the cycle from gaseous ions down to the solid.

low.restatement: Draw up for bond breaking (atomisation, ionisation), down for electron gain, formation and lattice closure; the cycle must balance by Hess's law.
low.analogy: A climbing wall: every upward hold costs energy, every descent gives some back, and the route must return to the start.
low.examPointer: Draw arrows in the direction of the stated enthalpy sign - upward arrows for positives, downward for negatives.

medium.restatement: The cycle's geometry is its logic: each vertical step is one defined enthalpy change, so the closed loop enforces Hess's law without any new physics.
medium.analogy: A flight of stairs with landings labelled by species: any two landings connect by any route, and the total climb is the same.
medium.examPointer: Displace the electron-affinity step sideways on paper purely for readability - the energy bookkeeping is unchanged.

options.text: A direct measurement of lattice energy

check.stem: State the enthalpy values shown in the sodium chloride construction for atomisation, ionisation, electron affinity and formation.
check.modelAnswer: Atomisation of Na +108, of half Cl2 +121, first ionisation of Na +500, electron affinity of Cl -364, and formation of NaCl -411 kJ mol^-1.

check.stem: State where the elements sit on a Born-Haber diagram.
check.modelAnswer: About a third of the way up, marked by a horizontal starting level.

check.stem: Explain why the Born-Haber cycle can deliver a lattice enthalpy that no experiment measures directly.
check.modelAnswer: Hess's law makes the enthalpy change route-independent: the direct gaseous-ion route equals the sum of the measurable atomisation, ionisation, electron-affinity and formation steps, so the closed loop solves for the one unmeasurable term.

check.stem: Sketch the level order for the potassium chloride cycle: which steps climb and which descend?
check.modelAnswer: Atomisation of K (+90) and of half Cl2 (+122) and ionisation of K (+418) climb; electron affinity of Cl (-349), formation (-437) and lattice formation descend, closing the loop.

lessons.title: Hess's law arithmetic on the cycle
lessons.opening: Once drawn, the cycle reduces to one subtraction: lattice enthalpy equals formation enthalpy minus the sum of every step that turned elements into gaseous ions. Mind the stoichiometry - magnesium chloride doubles the chlorine-side terms - and the numbers drop out: KCl at -718, MgO at -3812 kJ mol^-1.
keyPoints: Applying Hess's law: delta f H = delta 1 H + delta latt H, where delta 1 H is the sum of all steps converting elements to gaseous ions.
Rearranged for lattice energy: delta latt H = delta f H - delta 1 H.
The stage asked for is always the direct route; write the enthalpy equation and rearrange for the unknown.
Stoichiometry can double or halve terms: for MgCl2 the first electron affinity of chlorine is counted twice, adding electrons to two moles of chlorine atoms.
KCl: delta latt H = -437 - 90 - 122 - 418 + 349, which comes to -718 kJ mol^-1.
MgO: delta latt H = -602 - 148 - 248 - 736 - 1450 + 142 - 770, which comes to -3812 kJ mol^-1.

low.restatement: Lattice energy = formation minus the element-to-gaseous-ion sum; double terms for formula units with two of an ion; KCl: -437 - 281 = -718.
low.analogy: A taxi fare split: the total journey price minus the leg everyone shares leaves the private leg.
low.examPointer: Bracket every sum before subtracting - sign slips are the top mark-loser here.

medium.restatement: The cycle's arithmetic is a directed ledger: formation is the shortcut; the long route's steps must be listed with their signs and multiplicities, then subtracted.
medium.analogy: Reconciling a bank statement: the closing balance minus every listed transaction reveals the one unlisted fee.
medium.examPointer: Any stage can be the unknown - lattice, formation, or an ionisation - the rearrangement logic is identical.

check.stem: The rearranged equation for lattice energy is

Delta latt H = delta 1 H - delta f H
options.explanation: The subtraction runs the wrong way.

options.text: Delta latt H = delta f H + delta 1 H
options.explanation: The long route subtracts from the shortcut.

options.text: Delta latt H = delta f H x delta 1 H

check.stem: For MgCl2, the chlorine electron affinity is counted twice because

options.text: Two moles of chlorine atoms each gain one mole of electrons per mole of compound
options.explanation: The formula unit carries two chlorides.
Stoichiometry, not magnitude, drives the doubling.
Magnesium's two ionisations are separate terms.
It holds one magnesium per formula unit.

check.stem: The lattice energy of KCl from delta f H = -437, atomisation 90 and 122, ionisation +418 and electron affinity -349 is

options.explanation: That adds instead of subtracting the ion steps.
That adds every magnitude regardless of sign.

check.stem: The lattice energy of MgO is much more exothermic than KCl's chiefly because

options.text: Doubly charged, smaller ions and two electron affinities (one strongly endothermic) enter the ledger
options.explanation: Charge, size and stoichiometry all deepen the value.

options.text: Identify the direct and indirect routes, then rearrange the same equation for the unknown
options.explanation: The logic is symmetric whichever stage is hidden.

check.modelAnswer: Hess's law equates the direct one-step change with the sum of the multi-step route; the question's unknown sits on the direct side, so subtracting the known long-route terms isolates it.

check.stem: A cycle for calcium chloride uses delta f H = -796 kJ mol^-1, atomisation of Ca +178, of half Cl2 +121, first two ionisations +590 and +1146, and first electron affinity of Cl -349 (twice). Compute the lattice energy.

glossary.definition: A Hess's law energy cycle for ionic compounds, built from atomisation, ionisation, electron affinity, formation and lattice steps.
The enthalpy change forming 1 mole of a compound from its elements in standard states.
The enthalpy change forming the ionic solid from its gaseous ions, calculable from the cycle.

workedExample.prompt: Given the Born-Haber data for potassium chloride - delta f H = -437 kJ mol^-1, atomisation of K +90, atomisation of half Cl2 +122, first ionisation of K +418, first electron affinity of Cl -349 - calculate the lattice energy.
steps: Write the long route: formation equals the atomisation, ionisation and electron-affinity terms plus the lattice step.
Sum the element-to-gaseous-ion terms: 90 + 122 + 418 - 349 = 281 kJ mol^-1.
Apply delta latt H = delta f H - delta 1 H: (-437) - (+281).
workedExample.finalAnswer: The lattice energy of KCl is -718 kJ mol^-1.
